title: Michelle Yeoh Didn't Just Break The Oscars — She Broke Bones, Barriers, And Bond Girl Stereotypes First
dek: From a ballet dream cut short by a spinal injury to becoming the first Asian Best Actress winner in Academy history, here's the career you didn't know you didn't fully know.

items.heading: Before The Fight Scenes, There Was A Ballet Dream That Got Cut Short
items.text: Michelle Yeoh trained to become a professional ballet dancer, but a spinal injury ended that path before it began — which is how she ended up, almost by accident, in beauty pageants instead. She won Miss World Malaysia in 1983 at just 20 years old and went on to represent her country at Miss World in London.

images.caption: Long before Evelyn Wang, she was a ballet student sidelined by injury

items.heading: Then She Went And Became A Hong Kong Action Star Who Did Her Own Everything
items.text: After a Jackie Chan commercial got her noticed, Yeoh landed the lead in 1985's Yes, Madam, performing her own stunts in the male-dominated 'girls-with-guns' genre. After a brief retirement for marriage, she came roaring back for Supercop and Wing Chun, training relentlessly to pull off fights nobody expected from a former beauty queen.

images.caption: Yeoh training hard to become a genuine martial arts lead

items.heading: That Truck-To-Car Stunt In Supercop? She Really Did That
items.text: In Police Story 3: Supercop, Yeoh's character jumps from a moving truck onto a convertible driven by Jackie Chan as both vehicles speed down a highway — no stunt double, no visible wires. Quentin Tarantino later called the film's stuntwork the greatest ever filmed in any movie, and Yeoh has admitted the sequence very nearly went badly wrong on the first take.

images.caption: The stunt Tarantino couldn't stop talking about
Her Supercop co-star and longtime collaborator

items.heading: She Was One Of The First Bond Girls Who Actually Got To Fight Like Bond
items.text: As Wai Lin in Tomorrow Never Dies, Yeoh played a spy treated as 007's genuine equal instead of someone waiting to be rescued, performing all of her own fight choreography. Director Roger Spottiswoode wouldn't let her do every stunt herself for insurance reasons, but the hand-to-hand combat you see on screen is all her.

images.caption: Wai Lin, the Bond 'girl' who fought as an equal
Her 007 co-star in Tomorrow Never Dies

items.heading: For Crouching Tiger, She Took A Year Off Just To Train — Then Tore Her ACL Anyway
items.text: Yeoh deliberately didn't work for an entire year before filming Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon so she could focus on martial arts training and learning Mandarin for the role. The cast performed almost all of their own wire-assisted stunts, with VFX later erasing the rigging, but Yeoh still tore her ACL during an early fight scene and had to be flown to the U.S. for surgery mid-shoot.

images.caption: A year of training, one torn ACL, and cinema history

items.heading: Then, Decades Later, She Made Oscar History
items.text: For Everything Everywhere All at Once, Yeoh became the first Asian woman to win the Best Actress Oscar in the Academy's 95-year history. In her acceptance speech, she told the audience, "For all the little boys and girls who look like me watching tonight, this is a beacon of hope and possibilities."

images.caption: The role that finally brought her the Oscar

items.heading: She's Also Been Quietly Producing Movies Behind The Camera For Decades
items.text: Through her own production company, Mythical Films, Yeoh produced her first two English-language films, The Touch and Silver Hawk, both of which won her Huabiao Awards for Outstanding Co-Production Film. It's a whole side of her career that gets buried under the stunt reels.

images.caption: One of the films she produced through her own company
Her first producing credit, released in 2002
